title: A reproducible first run and a method for getting unstuck
summary: Use mise, Cargo, and a nine-step investigation to distinguish shell, compiler, and program failures.
objectives: Verify the active toolchain without changing a global default
Read commands as a chain of boundaries
Record an evidence-based investigation
body:
Purpose and the first useful model

Your first deliverable is a reproducible calculator run, accompanied by an investigation that another learner can repeat. A terminal command is a request to several programs. The shell first divides text into arguments. mise chooses tools from project configuration. Cargo selects a package, builds it if necessary, and starts a binary. The binary parses the arguments that survive those earlier steps. A failure at one boundary can resemble a failure somewhere else. Learning the boundaries gives you a way to solve unfamiliar problems without memorizing every diagnostic.

This course uses mise. The course mise.toml pins Rust 1.99.1, the stable point release announced on October 15, 2026. Begin in the course root, the folder containing index.html, mise.toml, scripts and projects; its folder name may differ from rust-course. The launch guide lists the mise, Python 3.11+, Git and native development-tool prerequisites. Open and inspect mise.toml before trusting it: it selects the pinned Rust version, a shared local build directory, and local Python tasks. Then run the setup and version commands below. rustup may be the underlying mechanism used to manage the Rust toolchain; it is not a reason to change your global default. The matching rust-toolchain.toml records the same version for Rust-aware tools. If these disagree, stop to inspect configuration instead of updating dependencies until the error disappears.

pwd
ls
mise trust
mise install
mise exec -- rustc --version
mise exec -- cargo --version
cd projects
mise exec -- cargo run -p workshop-calculator -- 12m + 3m

The final line should print 15m. Cargo may also print compilation messages to standard error. The double dash ends Cargo's arguments; the following three arguments belong to the calculator. A successful command is evidence that this package builds and this case works. It does not establish that every project, every boundary case, or an arbitrary future Rust version works. Keep that distinction visible in your notes from the beginning.

Prediction before running

Predict what happens if the command omits Cargo's double dash: mise exec -- cargo run -p workshop-calculator 12m + 3m. Does the calculator receive three operands, report an unknown operator, or fail to start? Write both your answer and which program you think produces the error. Then run the command. Expected result: Cargo rejects the unexpected arguments before the calculator starts. The operand text never reaches our program. This is why a calculator patch cannot fix this particular reproduction.

Now predict the result of the correctly separated command with 12m + 3s. Expected result: the binary starts, prints a units error to standard error, and exits unsuccessfully. Cargo did its job. Our domain deliberately rejects adding a length and a time. A nonzero exit is sometimes the correct implementation of the requested behavior. The first question is always what behavior the contract requires.

The problem-solving playbook: a worked investigation

Keep the playbook reference beside your terminal. The following investigation models its complete loop; later lessons remove some of the prompts so you choose the next experiment yourself.

Step 1 — state expected and actual behavior precisely. Expected: three calculator arguments produce 15m. Actual for the missing-separator command: Cargo reports an unexpected argument; no quantity is printed. Avoid writing only “Rust is broken.” That phrase hides both the action and the observable difference.

Step 2 — reproduce with exact context. Record the working directory rust-course/projects, the full command, the output, and the output of mise exec -- rustc --version. The intended version begins with rustc 1.99.1. If yours differs, that is an observation, not permission to assume it caused the argument error. Record the active Cargo version too. Reproduction is a controlled description, not a collection of screenshots with missing context.

Step 3 — locate the boundary. The message names Cargo's command syntax, so investigate Cargo-to-binary argument forwarding. Step 4 — read evidence rather than only the last line. Cargo help describes the separator before executable arguments. The reference binary expects exactly three arguments after its own executable name. These facts narrow the search before any source edit.

Step 5 — separate competing hypotheses. Hypothesis A: the toolchain cannot compile the project. Hypothesis B: arguments are being interpreted by Cargo. A remains plausible until a normal run builds; B predicts that inserting one separator will change which program responds. We have not yet proved either hypothesis merely by naming it.

Step 6 — make one distinguishing experiment. Add only the double dash and keep package, directory, operands, and tool version constant. Expected experimental result: the normal command builds or reuses its build and prints 15m. This disproves A as the explanation for this reproduction, while supporting B. It does not prove that the installation can never fail for another package.

Step 7 — apply the smallest sound fix. Correct the documented invocation; do not rewrite argument parsing to accommodate an argument list that never arrived. Step 8 — regress and state limits. Run the good addition, an incompatible-unit case, and the package tests. These checks cover routing into the binary and some calculator contracts, not arbitrary shell quoting or operating-system behavior.

Step 9 — capture the result. Write a short note: “Missing Cargo separator; observed Cargo argument rejection; changed only --; calculator then produced 15m; recorded Rust 1.99.1; package tests still need to be run or their actual result attached.” Distinguish an expected example from a command you actually executed. This habit makes your later debugging notes usable evidence.

Guided checkpoint

Read the small entry point below. Identify where argument count becomes a usage error, where calculation errors become exit code 1, and where success becomes exit code 0. Trace 12m + 3m through those branches on paper before running the test command. The library is responsible for quantities; the entry point is responsible for interaction with a process. Keeping those responsibilities separate allows unit tests without launching a terminal.

mise exec -- cargo test -p workshop-calculator
mise exec -- cargo run -p workshop-calculator -- 12m + 3s

When you get stuck: independent work and tiered help

Make a three-row evidence table for a good invocation, missing operand, and division by zero. Record producing component, expected exit status, actual status, and output stream. Quote multiplication as '*' so the shell does not expand it into filenames. A review request should include the exact command and a single disputed conclusion: “I think the shell expanded the star before Cargo; what experiment would distinguish that from a parser error?”

Hint 1: choose the next observation

count argument boundaries before reading calculator internals.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

compare the CLI integration test with the command that failed.

Worked solution

use mise exec -- cargo run -p workshop-calculator -- 4 '*' 3. The quotes are interpreted by the shell and the binary receives the one-character operator. A request to AI should ask for competing explanations and a distinguishing experiment before requesting a patch; verify the proposed command against help and observed output.

Review and mastery evidence

The recommended workflow records the responsible program, the changed factor, and the reason the corrected invocation works. Reading Cargo help is the right abstraction for argument forwarding; an argument-parsing dependency would solve a different problem inside the binary. An alternative is to run the already-built executable directly when isolating Cargo from process behavior, while remembering to rebuild after source changes. Choose that experiment when the build/launch boundary is uncertain.

title: Values, expressions, and choosing arithmetic behavior
summary: Build a reliable integer model before adding parsing and units.
objectives: Distinguish bindings, values, types, and expressions
Choose checked arithmetic deliberately
Use boundary examples to explain overflow and division
body:
Purpose: make numbers mean something

A calculator is small enough to understand completely and rich enough to expose important design choices. Its numbers are signed 64-bit integers. That means a finite representable range, exact integer results within that range, and a need to define behavior when the mathematical result does not fit. Saying “it adds numbers” is not a complete contract. Decide whether to reject overflow, wrap, saturate, or use an arbitrary-precision representation. This project rejects overflow because silently changing a measurement would mislead its user.

A binding gives a name to a value. The type determines what operations are available and what those operations mean. let count = 3_i64 creates an i64 value and an immutable binding. let mut permits assigning a new value through that binding; it does not make an integer infinitely large. Shadowing creates another binding, potentially with a different type. Use shadowing for a clear transformation, such as text to parsed quantity, and mutation for state that changes over time. These are design choices with different explanations.

Runnable model and prediction

Run these cases from rust-course/projects. Before running them, write the expected value or error and explain whether parsing, arithmetic, or formatting should decide it. Quoting the star protects it from shell expansion. The double dash forwards arguments to the binary.

mise exec -- cargo run -p workshop-calculator -- -7 / 2
mise exec -- cargo run -p workshop-calculator -- 9223372036854775807 + 1
mise exec -- cargo run -p workshop-calculator -- 8 '*' -3

Expected results are -3, an overflow error, and -24. Integer division truncates toward zero; it does not round to the nearest integer or compute a floating-point decimal. A value that prints as -3 is therefore correct for this contract. If the product required physical measurements with fractions, changing the numeric model would be a requirements decision, not merely a display adjustment. Give every surprising result a contract before judging it.

An expression evaluates to a value. A block can be an expression when its final expression is not followed by a semicolon. For example, let doubled = { let base = 4; base * 2 }; binds 8. Adding a semicolon after base * 2 changes the block result to (), the unit value. Unit means the expression provides no useful payload; it is not the same thing as a quantity's meters or seconds. Rust uses similar English words for different concepts, so read the type in context.

Guided checkpoint: preserve the failure

Read Quantity::apply in the reference. checked_add returns Some(result) or None. The code converts None into CalcError::Overflow with ok_or, keeping the reason a calculation failed available to its caller. Returning zero instead would make failure indistinguishable from a real zero result. Panicking would hand ordinary user input to a mechanism intended for a violated program assumption. Result is the appropriate shape when the caller should choose how to report a recoverable failure.

Complete the calculator scaffold one operation at a time. First parse signed scalar integers and support checked addition, returning a Result from the first runnable checkpoint. Make an ordinary successful-addition test pass, then add the maximum-plus-one assertion and verify it returns Overflow through the same checked implementation. Only after both work should you add units. This sequence creates a feedback loop in which a failure has a small likely cause. The full reference is a worked checkpoint; compare control flow after your own attempt rather than typing it without predictions.

Intentional mistake: debug success is not a policy

Temporarily write an isolated expression using ordinary addition of two runtime i64 values. A tempting claim is that Rust always panics on overflow. Overflow behavior depends on operation and compiler settings; debug checks are not a substitute for your public arithmetic contract. Do not teach a release-only behavior accidentally. checked_add expresses the choice directly and keeps it consistent across build profiles. Restore the scaffold to checked operations after observing the experiment.

Another tempting mistake is checking only a divisor equal to zero. i64::MIN divided by -1 also cannot fit in i64. The reference checks zero separately for its specific error and uses checked_div to detect the remaining overflow. Designing distinct errors does not require duplicating all arithmetic implementation details. Let a documented primitive enforce the range boundary.

Playbook application: a surprising negative quotient

Observation: -7 divided by 2 produces -3. Hypothesis A: the parser lost the minus sign. Hypothesis B: the program performs integer division with truncation toward zero. A distinguishing experiment is -8 divided by 2, followed by -7 multiplied by 1. Expected results are -4 and -7. Those results disprove the lost-sign explanation for these inputs while fitting B. Inspect checked_div documentation to connect the evidence to a specified rule. Changing output formatting would not repair a numeric-model mismatch.

For your investigation, record where information could first diverge: command arguments, parsed numeric values, arithmetic result, or formatted text. If you add temporary debug output, print to standard error and remove it after the experiment. One-factor experiments become less useful when you simultaneously change the type, parser, and operation. Ask AI to explain both candidate models and predict each experiment, then compare its claims with the actual command output.

Reconstruct the complete early checkpoint

This complete early checkpoint parses two scalar values and performs checked addition. It deliberately precedes units, other operators, and the CLI argument boundary. The checkpoint contract and source are separately preserved. From the course root, run:

python3 scripts/start-checkpoint.py p01 01-checked-add
cd learner-work/checkpoints/p01-calculator/01-checked-add
mise exec -- cargo test
mise exec -- cargo run

The helper refuses an existing destination; choose a new explicit destination if you already have work there. This is a complete guided comparison checkpoint, not evidence that you independently implemented the project. Make predictions, inspect each boundary test, then carry the next requirement into your own source. A separately named final checkpoint reconstructs the current complete reference without pretending it is this earlier milestone. Exact reconstruction and test commands are recorded in the author check log.

When you get stuck: independent work and tiered help

Add table-driven cases for negative addition, zero multiplication, equal negative operands, i64 minimum subtraction, and minimum divided by -1. For every case, name the contract being tested. Then explain why adding 1 to an unsigned maximum differs from parsing a negative number into an unsigned type: the first concerns arithmetic, the second input representation. Do not merge these into a vague “bad number” story in your design notes.

Hint 1: choose the next observation

inspect the exact method return type with the standard-library documentation.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

write a match over Some and None before using combinators.

Worked solution

self.value.checked_add(rhs.value).ok_or(CalcError::Overflow) preserves either the exact result or the explicit domain error. A useful review request is “Here are my boundary cases; which arithmetic failure can still escape as a panic?” Include the relevant branch, not the entire repository.

Recommended design and alternatives

A clear match expression is a good first implementation. Using ok_or becomes idiomatic when it shortens a direct Option-to-Result conversion without hiding a decision. Using several nested combinators merely to avoid local names is not an improvement. The reference's intermediate unit and value variables make the two independent questions visible: is this operation dimensionally permitted, and does its numeric result fit?

Mastery means explaining the value of every expression in one successful and one failing path, including the Result wrapper. Passing tests over a few small numbers is evidence about those cases. Boundary tests add evidence about representational edges, but still do not prove every property over every i64. You should be able to identify a missing case and justify why it matters before claiming the calculator is complete.

title: Build a checked calculator with units and useful errors
summary: Finish a small program whose types, parser, library, and CLI share one explicit contract.
objectives: Represent a closed set of units with an enum
Separate parsing, domain operations, and process behavior
Test unsupported operations and exit statuses
body:
Purpose and design boundary

The complete calculator accepts exactly three arguments: a quantity, an operator, and another quantity. A quantity is a signed i64 with an optional m or s suffix. No suffix means a scalar. This is deliberately a small language: 2m is valid, 2.5m is not, and kilograms are not recognized. A narrow documented contract lets you complete a program rather than expand forever into a general scientific calculator. Your deliverable includes the behavior, tests, and a short explanation of what remains outside the model.

Model the unit as an enum because exactly three states are supported. A string can contain any text, so a function accepting arbitrary strings must repeatedly ask whether those strings are recognized. Once parsing constructs Unit::Meters, later code can rely on that recognized state. A Quantity groups value and unit so callers cannot accidentally pass the numeric part while losing the dimension. Public fields keep this first model simple; later projects use private fields where construction invariants require stronger protection.

Prediction: valid syntax can still be invalid meaning

Predict these operations before execution: 3m * 2, 3m * 2m, 8s / 2s, and 8 / 2s. The expected answers are 6m, an incompatible-unit error, 4, and an incompatible-unit error. All operands can be parsed. The failures concern the deliberately supported dimensional algebra. The program has no square-meter or inverse-second unit. Rejecting those expressions honestly is better than silently returning a result with an incorrect unit.

mise exec -- cargo run -p workshop-calculator -- 3m '*' 2
mise exec -- cargo run -p workshop-calculator -- 3m '*' 2m
mise exec -- cargo run -p workshop-calculator -- 8s / 2s
mise exec -- cargo test -p workshop-calculator

Guided build: three functions, three responsibilities

Start with parsing. FromStr for Quantity receives borrowed text and either produces a complete Quantity or CalcError::InvalidNumber. strip_suffix identifies an allowed suffix without indexing into UTF-8 by guessed character positions. Parsing the remainder as i64 delegates integer syntax and range checks to the standard library. The reference rejects surrounding whitespace explicitly, so command-line quotes cannot quietly change the language. Parsing is a boundary where untrusted text becomes a constrained domain value.

Next implement Quantity::apply. For addition and subtraction, require identical units before arithmetic. For multiplication, preserve the non-scalar unit if either operand is scalar. For division, preserve the left unit when the divisor is scalar, and cancel equal units to Scalar. Write the accepted table before writing match arms. The type checker ensures that every enum pattern you actually match is handled; it does not invent the correct dimensional rules for you.

Finally connect calculate and the entry point. calculate composes parsing and applying with ?. The question-mark operator returns early on an error; it does not swallow the error or make the operation infallible. main chooses how to present the result and which exit status to return. The reference prints successful output on standard output and errors on standard error so other programs can consume the successful result without scraping messages.

The entry point receives native operating-system arguments with args_os and explicitly accepts only valid UTF-8 calculator text. Invalid text becomes a usage error rather than an implicit panic in argument collection. Later file-based projects preserve native path values and convert only fields whose grammar requires text. This is a boundary decision already present in the recommended first project.

Intentional mistake and a focused repair

Introduce a bug only in your learner copy: allow any multiplication and keep the left unit. Then 3m * 2m becomes 6m, which is numerically plausible and dimensionally wrong. A test that checks only the number 6 misses the defect. Repair the rule before changing formatting. Add an assertion on the full result, including its unit or its specific error. The lesson is broader than physical units: tests must observe the part of the contract you could violate.

A second mistake is accepting an unknown operator by treating it as addition. This produces a reasonable-looking answer for invalid input. Exhaustive matching of known operators with an explicit error fallback makes the boundary visible. Unknown input should not select a successful operation accidentally. If you later add exponentiation, specify its unit and overflow behavior before adding a new branch.

Playbook: distinguish parsing from dimensional rules

Observation: 3m * 2m fails while 3m * 2 succeeds. Hypothesis A: the parser cannot read m suffixes. Hypothesis B: the multiplication rule rejects two dimensional operands. Keep the first operand and operator fixed; vary only the second suffix. Expected result: the scalar case succeeds. Then run 3m + 2m, expected 5m. These observations disprove A for m-suffixed integers and support B. The relevant code boundary is Quantity::apply, not FromStr.

For the investigation record, quote '*' in both commands so shell expansion cannot become a confounding variable. Record whether the message says invalid number or incompatible units. A label is useful evidence only if the implementation maps errors faithfully; inspect the branch once the experiment narrows it. Ask an AI reviewer to propose a test that would distinguish a swapped-unit bug from numeric overflow. Require its predicted outcomes before running the test.

Output failures belong to the first CLI contract

The calculation can succeed while writing its answer fails. In src/main.rs, run returns io::Result<ExitCode>: it preserves usage status 2 and domain status 1 when diagnostics can be written, while fallible writeln! and flush propagate sink failures. Main makes one best-effort diagnostic attempt and returns failure even if stderr is also closed. Do not replace these calls with println! to shorten the code; that changes an ordinary broken pipe into a panic. The actual child-process tests close the pipe's only reader before starting the calculator, which removes a scheduling race from the experiment.

The early checked-add executable needs to report either its typed arithmetic error or an output error. Its Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> boundary can carry either error to process termination. Box owns that error value, and dyn Error means any type implementing the standard error interface; Stage 2 explains these types fully. This small executable boundary does not erase the library's Number versus Overflow distinction.

When you get stuck: independent work and tiered help

Implement a remainder operator in your scaffold under an explicit contract: same-unit operands produce a remainder in that unit; a zero divisor is rejected; overflow is handled with checked_rem. Write examples for negative operands and explain Rust's remainder behavior. Do not silently broaden multiplication while making this unrelated change. This is a design exercise: the supplied reference intentionally remains the four-operation calculator, so your extension should have its own review note.

When you get stuck, first reduce to a scalar input and an existing operator.

Hint 1: choose the next observation

inspect whether the failure precedes or follows construction of Quantity.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

write the accepted unit pairs as a table and match that table.

Worked solution for the original checkpoint

match '+' and '-' together, reject unequal units, call the corresponding checked operation, then construct Quantity only after ok_or succeeds. For remainder, the same-unit guard is reusable, but the numeric method changes. Bring a reviewer the proposed rule, one success, one zero-divisor case, and one negative example.

Review, evidence, and mastery

The recommended implementation gives parsing to FromStr, presentation to Display, and domain operations to a small library. These standard traits express familiar concepts and support testing without launching a process. Direct helper functions would also be sound for a private one-off calculation, but the public parse and formatting interfaces are useful here. A command-line parsing library becomes worthwhile when options, subcommands, or generated help replace the current exact three-argument contract.

Your mastery demonstration is a short change request: explain the current grammar, add a justified test, implement one well-scoped extension, and identify a non-goal. Run both unit tests and the CLI check after the change. Passing them demonstrates the asserted cases and process behavior; it does not establish a complete physical-units system. Explain that limit in the README as part of the implementation rather than treating it as an embarrassing omission.

Engineering decisions and evidence

Requirements and invariants

Three CLI arguments describe signed i64 quantities and one supported operator. Every successful result has a supported unit and representable numeric value. Addition and subtraction require equal units; products need a scalar; equal units cancel during division. Ordinary invalid input returns a typed error and a nonzero exit, without panicking.

Chosen design and concrete habits

Quantity and Unit carry the domain model; FromStr handles text; checked arithmetic enforces range; Display presents quantities and errors; main owns stdout, stderr, and exit status. The first runnable checkpoint already uses Result-based failure handling. Documentation examples propagate errors with ?, and assertion-only test unwraps express known expected successes. No dependency is needed to express this small contract.

Meaningful alternative and evolution threshold

A dimensional type system or units library would prevent more combinations statically, at the cost of a more complex generic model. Adopt one when quantities enter a larger scientific calculation or compound dimensions are required. A CLI framework becomes justified by options and subcommands; fractional measurements require a deliberately specified numeric representation, not a formatting patch.

Actual checks and remaining uncertainty

Native unit, CLI integration, and documentation tests passed in verification/native-tests.log. The patch audit reran all five foundation packages after documentation and CLI boundary changes; all 29 checks passed in verification/patch001-foundations-tests.log. Covered cases include overflow, minimum divided by -1, unit rejection, truncating division, argument count, and exit streams. Finite small-domain checks do not prove all i64 arithmetic or all shell invocations. Independent review is pending.

This checkpoint teaches the checked integer arithmetic branch. The next lesson adds an explicit fractional-length conversion command with a separate numeric contract; it does not silently change integer addition or division. The final reference entry point includes both commands, while each checkpoint names the branch under review.

title: Ownership as an API decision: borrow, move, or clone
summary: Use a task title to connect ownership rules to the actual lifetime of stored data.
objectives: Explain moves without calling them deep copies
Choose borrowed input and owned storage deliberately
Repair overlapping borrows by restructuring scope
body:
Purpose: a journal must keep data after input disappears

A task journal accepts text from command-line arguments and keeps titles in a collection. The command argument buffer and the journal have different jobs and potentially different lifetimes. This makes ownership a practical design question: who is responsible for retaining the title's allocation after the function returns? Do not begin with “how can I satisfy the borrow checker?” Begin with “which part of the program must keep this data?” The signature should express that answer.

String owns a growable UTF-8 text buffer. &str borrows a view into existing UTF-8 text. Moving a String transfers ownership of its allocation; it does not normally duplicate all the characters. Cloning creates another owned buffer and copies its contents. Borrowing lets code inspect existing data while the owner remains responsible for it. These three operations have different semantics even when the printed text looks identical. Avoid the inaccurate rule that Rust “always copies on assignment” or “never copies anything.”

Predict the ownership transition

In an isolated learner file, predict whether this compiles: let title = String::from("learn"); let stored = title; println!("{title}");. Expected result: use-after-move error E0382. Ownership moved into stored, so title cannot then be used as an owner. The bytes did not disappear; the old binding lost permission to access the value. Replacing the move with let stored = &title permits both reads, provided the borrow does not outlive title.

Run the supplied intentional error from rust-course/exercises/foundations. This fixture is supposed to fail and is not part of the reference workspace tests. Compare the primary code with expected-errors.json rather than expecting the entire English message to remain identical forever.

mkdir -p /tmp/rust-course-diagnostics
mise exec -- rustc --edition=2024 --emit=metadata --out-dir /tmp/rust-course-diagnostics 01-use-after-move.rs

Guided checkpoint: store one intentional copy

Read Journal::add. Its title argument is &str, which means callers can supply a string literal, a borrowed String, or another string slice without surrendering ownership. The method validates the text, chooses an identifier, and then uses to_owned when constructing Task. That allocation is intentional: the journal must retain its own title after add returns. A clone here has an explanation. Adding clones throughout the caller just to silence diagnostics would obscure the design.

Task::title returns &str borrowed from self. A reader can inspect the title without allocating another buffer. Journal::tasks returns a slice of tasks rather than the whole mutable Vec, preserving control over additions and state changes. Follow one title through these boundaries: borrowed incoming text, owned stored text, borrowed outgoing view. Draw the owners and views, and mark the point at which each view stops being used.

mise exec -- cargo test -p task-journal round_trip_and_transitions
mise exec -- cargo run -p task-journal -- reference/p02-journal/fixtures/tasks-v1.txt list

Mutation and the useful exclusivity rule

A mutable reference grants exclusive access for the duration of that borrow. You cannot keep two active mutable references to the same collection and use both later. The crucial word is active: the compiler often ends a borrow at its last use rather than at the enclosing closing brace. Read the actual sequence of uses instead of assuming every reference lasts to the end of a function. The second supplied fixture deliberately overlaps two mutable views of the same Vec.

In Journal::complete, iter_mut finds one task and gives exclusive access to that task while its status changes. The method then returns, ending that access before another caller can mutate the journal. This is a small, local ownership story. If an implementation instead returns a mutable Task and then tries to push another task while holding it, Vec reallocation and overlapping access become part of the problem. Prefer completing the mutation inside the method when the caller does not need a long-lived view.

Playbook: a borrow error after adding a task

Observation: code that saves a borrowed title, pushes a new task, and then prints the saved title is rejected. Hypothesis A: Rust forbids printing borrowed text. Hypothesis B: the saved view overlaps mutation of its owning collection. Distinguishing experiment: print the title before the push, leaving the same borrowed type and the same push. Expected result: the borrow ends at its last use, and the reordered sequence can compile. That disproves A and supports B for this control flow.

The smallest sound fix depends on the requirement. If the output must occur before mutation, reordering is enough. If a snapshot must survive mutation, an intentional owned copy is appropriate. If the caller only needs an identifier, store that small value and look up the task again afterward. There is no universal “always clone” or “never clone” repair. Ask an AI reviewer to compare these three requirements and explain the allocation and lifetime tradeoffs before accepting a patch.

When you get stuck: independent work and tiered help

Add a search method in your learner journal that returns borrowed titles containing a query. Decide whether the result should be a Vec of borrowed slices or an iterator. Either can be clear at this stage. Write a test that keeps the journal alive while reading results. Then intentionally try to return those views from a function that constructs a local journal. Explain why the returned references would have no living owner. Repair that second function by returning owned strings if the caller really needs independent results.

Hint 1: choose the next observation

underline every String and every &str, then name the owner for each borrowed slice.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

find the last use of a reference around the reported mutable operation.

Worked solution

accept title: &str, validate it, construct title: title.to_owned(), and expose fn title(&self) -> &str. This creates ownership exactly where persistence is required. A focused review request is “Does this allocation serve a storage requirement, or can the borrow end earlier?” Include the call site because signatures alone may hide the lifetime conflict.

Recommended design and alternatives and mastery

Accepting String and storing it is sound when the API intentionally transfers ownership. The reference accepts &str because callers may keep their input and the storage boundary can make one explicit owned copy. A generic Into<String> constructor can later support both transfer and conversion, but it should be introduced for demonstrated caller needs. Judge these alternatives by allocation, retention, and call-site clarity rather than by the number of generic parameters.

Mastery is the ability to repair both a move error and an overlapping borrow error while explaining the resulting data lifetime. Compiler acceptance establishes that the checked ownership rules hold for safe code in that program. It does not prove task validation, file durability, or performance. Keep those concerns separate so memory safety becomes a reliable foundation rather than an excuse to skip other evidence.

title: Model valid task states and make invalid transitions visible
summary: Turn informal journal rules into private fields, enums, constructors, and explicit failures.
objectives: Translate invariants into construction boundaries
Distinguish absence from failure
Test state transitions without filesystem IO
body:
Purpose: protect the meaning of a task

A task is more than three fields. It has an identifier greater than zero, a title with useful content, and a status chosen from a known set. The journal has another invariant: identifiers are unique within the current stored collection. These claims are requirements that must hold wherever data enters or changes. If every caller can set every field freely, every caller must remember every rule. A small domain API makes the rules easier to preserve and easier to test.

The reference stores Task fields privately and exposes read-only getters. Status is an enum with Open and Done. Journal owns a Vec<Task>, but its tasks method returns a slice. Callers can inspect tasks without inserting malformed rows. add, complete, and remove describe permitted state changes. None of these choices prevents all bugs automatically. They reduce the number of places where the invariants can be violated, which makes review and testing more focused.

Predict transitions before implementing

Create an empty journal, add one task, complete it twice, then try to complete identifier 99. Predict the number of tasks, the final status of the first task, and the last result. Expected: one task, Done, and Error::NotFound(99). Completing an already-completed task is idempotent in this contract: the second call leaves the state unchanged and succeeds. Another application might reject the second completion, but that would be a different explicit rule.

mise exec -- cargo test -p task-journal round_trip_and_transitions
mise exec -- cargo test -p task-journal rejects_corruption_without_partial_success

Do not confuse a missing task with a false status flag. Option can represent a lookup with no result. Result represents an operation that might fail and carries a reason. The complete method turns a failed lookup into NotFound using ok_or. Returning a bool would lose the distinction between “already done,” “identifier absent,” and “operation succeeded,” unless the contract carefully assigned meanings to those booleans. A named error is easier to review.

Guided checkpoint: validate before mutation

Implement add in the learner scaffold. First reject titles whose trimmed form is empty, whose UTF-8 byte length exceeds 200, or whose characters include a control character. The reference stores the original nonempty text rather than trimming it automatically. This is a deliberate policy: validation and normalization are separate operations. If you choose normalization for your extension, state it and test it. The length bound counts bytes, so a non-ASCII character may use more than one byte.

Next enforce the maximum task count. Then compute the next identifier with checked_add. Finally push the newly built Task. The order matters because all ordinary validation failures occur before mutation. A caller receiving an error can rely on no task having been added. This is a small transaction-like property within memory, not a database transaction. Write an assertion that the collection remains empty after rejected input, instead of checking only that an error was returned.

Intentional mistake: replacing an enum with an unrestricted string

In a scratch design, replace Status with String and allow callers to write any value. List the additional states you have now admitted: done, Done, complete, empty text, a typo, and arbitrary bytes representable as UTF-8. Every display and persistence branch must decide what those states mean. Restore the enum and observe that a match missing Done is rejected by the compiler. The supplied 04-nonexhaustive.rs exercise demonstrates this diagnostic. An exhaustive match is useful when adding a new state should force a review of existing behavior.

A wildcard arm can hide that pressure. Match arms ending in _ are appropriate when a fallback is the intended behavior, but adding them automatically just to satisfy the compiler can conceal forgotten business rules. For our status representation, handling both named variants explicitly is clearer. If you add Archived later, the compiler should direct you to the places that need a deliberate decision.

Playbook: a title looks short but is rejected

Observation: a title consisting of repeated emoji reaches the 200-byte limit before it reaches 200 visible symbols. Hypothesis A: the limit uses character count and contains an off-by-one bug. Hypothesis B: the specified limit counts UTF-8 bytes. A distinguishing experiment compares the same count of ASCII letters and a multibyte symbol, then measures each with .len() and .chars().count(). Expected result: byte lengths differ while the scalar-value counts match. That disproves A as the explanation for this case.

The correct fix is not automatically to replace len. Decide what the product limit is meant to protect. A storage byte limit directly bounds encoded data. A user-facing character limit raises additional questions about grapheme clusters and Unicode normalization. For this course the byte rule is documented and tested. Improve the error text if the observation shows it is confusing; changing semantics without a requirement would make the tests and file contract inconsistent.

Reconstruct the complete early checkpoint

This complete early checkpoint contains private owned task state and validated transitions, with a 32-task cap. It deliberately precedes encoding and file I/O; the final project documents its larger cap separately. The checkpoint contract and source are separately preserved. From the course root, run:

python3 scripts/start-checkpoint.py p02 01-domain
cd learner-work/checkpoints/p02-journal/01-domain
mise exec -- cargo test
mise exec -- cargo run

The helper refuses an existing destination; choose a new explicit destination if you already have work there. This is a complete guided comparison checkpoint, not evidence that you independently implemented the project. Make predictions, inspect each boundary test, then carry the next requirement into your own source. A separately named final checkpoint reconstructs the current complete reference without pretending it is this earlier milestone. Exact reconstruction and test commands are recorded in the author check log.

When you get stuck: independent work and tiered help

Add rename(id, title) to your learner journal. Reuse the existing validation rule, return NotFound for an absent identifier, and guarantee that a failed rename leaves the old title intact. Decide and document which error wins if both the identifier is missing and the proposed title is invalid. Either ordering can be defensible; it should be consistent and covered by a test. This task forces you to reason about both validation boundaries and observable failure precedence.

Hint 1: choose the next observation

write before-and-after states before writing the method.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

validate the new value into a temporary variable before assigning to the task.

Worked solution

call validate_title, find the task with iter_mut and ok_or, then replace the stored title with title.to_owned(). The borrowed input must become owned storage once, after acceptance. Ask for a review of the invariant and error ordering, not “make this more Rusty.” An AI can suggest alternatives, but you should reject any that silently alter the transition contract.

Review and mastery evidence

The recommended domain boundary enforces title rules for every construction route and exposes private fields through read-only views. The decoder separately enforces collection rules such as unique identifiers. A dedicated validated Title type would be a sound next step if several domain objects shared the same title invariant; for one Task model, a private validation helper keeps the requirement visible without unnecessary indirection. Keep per-value and collection invariants distinct in either design.

Mastery means you can enumerate valid states, identify every constructor or mutator, and provide a test for each rejection that must preserve old state. Passing the compiler's exhaustiveness check proves that your match covers the enum variants, not that the actions in those arms satisfy the requirements. Unit tests add behavioral evidence. A concise design note should connect each invariant to its enforcing boundary and acknowledge that identifier reuse after deleting the highest task is allowed by this reference's current-file model.

title: A versioned text format that rejects corruption
summary: Persist task meaning without quietly accepting duplicate identifiers or unknown file versions.
objectives: Specify a file grammar and version policy
Separate parsing from file access
Test round trips and corrupt inputs independently
body:
Purpose: yesterday's bytes become today's input

A journal becomes useful when tasks survive process exit. Persistence introduces a new trust boundary: bytes on disk may be missing, truncated, edited by hand, or written by an older program. Treat loading as validation of external input, even if your program originally produced the file. Reusing in-memory assumptions without checking them can turn corrupted data into plausible task state. The goal is a format small enough to inspect and strict enough to reject ambiguity.

Our format starts with TASKS, a tab, and version 1. Each following row contains an unsigned identifier, a status word, and a title, separated by tabs. Titles cannot contain control characters, so tabs and newlines cannot escape into new fields or rows. UTF-8 text is allowed, and the title limit counts bytes. The decoder accepts the supported header and known status strings only. A future format version must have a deliberate migration; it must not be guessed from data that happens to look familiar.

Prediction: a round trip is not the whole contract

Predict what happens for each fixture: the valid tasks-v1.txt file, the duplicate-identifier fixture, an empty file, and a file with TASKS version 2. Expected: the valid file decodes; the other three fail. An empty file is different from a missing path. Missing can mean “new journal”; present but empty indicates a malformed stored journal. This distinction protects users from a damaged file silently appearing to erase all their tasks.

mise exec -- cargo test -p task-journal checked_in_fixture_roundtrips
mise exec -- cargo run -p task-journal -- reference/p02-journal/fixtures/tasks-v1.txt list
mise exec -- cargo run -p task-journal -- reference/p02-journal/fixtures/corrupt-duplicate.txt list

A round-trip assertion decode(encode(journal)) == journal verifies that the two functions agree for that journal. It does not prove that the format is unambiguous or that malformed input is rejected. Two functions can share the same bug and round-trip perfectly. Keep explicit fixtures with independently understood contents and separate rejection tests for missing fields, extra fields, duplicate IDs, invalid status, and unsupported versions.

Guided checkpoint: build a decoder that commits at the end

Start with a pure decode(&str) function so parsing tests need no filesystem. Check the byte limit and header before reading rows. For each row, require exactly three columns. Parse the identifier, reject zero, track previously seen IDs in a HashSet, decode status, and validate the title. Build a local Journal and return it only after all rows succeed. If row 40 fails, the caller receives an error instead of a partly loaded collection of 39 tasks.

The HashSet is not merely an optimization. It records a collection-wide invariant during decoding. Task alone cannot know whether its identifier duplicates another task. Keep that check at the journal boundary. Likewise, row numbers belong to the decoder because they describe source structure, while title validity belongs to the title-validation helper because both user input and persisted rows need the same rule.

Read encode after decode. It emits a stable header, a known status spelling, and the original title. Writing into a String is an in-memory formatting operation; its expect call documents an invariant of that destination rather than dismissing ordinary disk failure. Actual File writes return IO errors elsewhere. Two operations both named “write” can have different failure models, which is why you should inspect the destination type before judging error handling.

Intentional mistake: silently skip malformed rows

In a scratch decoder, replace a malformed-row error with continue. The program may appear more resilient because it loads the remaining rows. But its success result now conceals data loss. If the user saves the loaded journal, the skipped task disappears permanently from the new file. Tolerant ingestion is sometimes appropriate for an analytics pipeline; it needs explicit rejected-row accounting and recovery policy. A personal task store should not silently reinterpret corruption as successful loading.

Another mistake is regenerating every identifier while loading. Titles and statuses may still look correct, while commands referring to saved IDs target different tasks. Identifiers are part of this file's meaning. Preserve and validate them. Our add operation chooses one more than the current maximum, so removing the highest ID permits reuse; that is documented as a current-collection identity model rather than a globally permanent event identity.

Playbook: tasks disappear after reopening

Observation: a learner decoder returns fewer tasks than the fixture contains. Hypothesis A: the file reader truncated the bytes. Hypothesis B: the decoder silently skips a malformed row. Distinguishing experiment: call decode directly on a small inline string containing one valid row and one invalid row. Expected result for the reference: an error, with no partial Journal returned. If the learner implementation returns one task from the inline string, filesystem truncation is disproven for that reproduction.

Capture the smallest input that demonstrates the behavior and the exact row rule it violates. Do not begin by rewriting save. The boundary under investigation is bytes-to-domain-state, and the direct test bypasses unrelated file access. Ask an AI assistant to list what an observed row count can and cannot establish. A good answer should distinguish bytes read, rows recognized, and tasks accepted, and propose a measurement at the first uncertain boundary.

When you get stuck: independent work and tiered help

Design a version-2 format adding an optional priority. You do not need to replace the reference. Write a migration function from a valid version-1 Journal to a version-2 model, choose the default priority, and specify whether unknown versions are rejected. Include a fixture with a title containing non-ASCII text. Then write one test proving that a bad second row does not produce a partly loaded result. The exercise is about compatibility policy as much as string splitting.

Hint 1: choose the next observation

write the grammar in words and identify forbidden delimiter characters.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

separate parse_row from decode only if the helper gets a coherent contract.

Worked solution for the current checkpoint

decode into a local Vec, maintain a set of IDs, return Err immediately on any invalid field, and construct the final Journal after the loop. When requesting review, provide the format rules, one valid fixture, and two adversarial fixtures. Ask which ambiguity remains, not only whether the code is shorter.

Review and mastery evidence

The recommended parser treats persisted bytes as fallible input and returns a reason while leaving the original file intact. The hand-readable tab format is appropriate because titles exclude delimiters and the schema has three fields. A structured serialization library becomes worthwhile for nested data or external interoperability; it still would not choose duplicate-ID policy, migration behavior, or title rules. Those are domain requirements under either syntax.

Mastery means explaining how a file becomes a fully valid Journal, including what happens when the last row is corrupt. Demonstrate a round trip, an independently specified fixture, and an intentional rejection. State that these tests support the format contract but do not prove crash durability or safe concurrent access. Those are IO and coordination properties, addressed separately in the next checkpoint.

title: File IO: preserve errors and replace data carefully
summary: Complete a single-writer journal while explaining exactly what temporary-file replacement guarantees.
objectives: Differentiate NotFound from other IO failures
Bound reads before allocation grows without limit
Implement and test a temporary-file replacement protocol
body:
Purpose: storage is a protocol, not one write call

An in-memory journal can validate a title perfectly and still lose data through careless file handling. IO connects your process to resources whose behavior is not fully under its control: files can disappear, permissions can change, disks can fill, and another process may act concurrently. Your job is to choose a protocol and report its actual guarantees. This checkpoint implements a small single-writer store, not a database disguised as a text file.

The reference load operation opens the requested path. Only ErrorKind::NotFound becomes an empty Journal. PermissionDenied, invalid UTF-8, malformed content, and other failures remain errors. Treating all errors as “start fresh” turns a temporary access problem into an apparently empty task list. A subsequent save could overwrite data the program never read. Preserving the error protects both the user and your ability to diagnose the problem.

The CLI retains its file argument as an operating-system path. Task titles, commands, and identifiers are explicitly converted to UTF-8 text with recoverable errors when conversion fails. A filesystem path need not be valid Unicode, so converting every argument to String at process startup would impose an unnecessary assumption on file access.

Prediction and a safe runnable workflow

Use a scratch directory that you own. Do not mutate the checked-in fixture. Run the commands below from rust-course/projects after creating a directory named scratch in that directory. Predict each output and state change before running it. The first list has no task output because the path is missing. add prints added 1. Completing task 1 updates status; a later list shows [x].

mkdir -p scratch
mise exec -- cargo run -p task-journal -- scratch/tasks.txt list
mise exec -- cargo run -p task-journal -- scratch/tasks.txt add 'Practice careful IO'
mise exec -- cargo run -p task-journal -- scratch/tasks.txt done 1
mise exec -- cargo run -p task-journal -- scratch/tasks.txt list
mise exec -- cargo test -p task-journal --test storage

The expected output assumes a new scratch path. If it already exists, inspect it and choose another scratch filename instead of deleting data blindly. Reproducible experiments must control their initial state. The storage integration test creates a unique temporary directory and cleans up its own files; it does not depend on an already-populated personal journal.

Guided checkpoint: bounded loading

Before decoding, load reads at most one byte beyond the 1 MiB limit. The extra byte distinguishes a file exactly at the accepted limit from a larger file. Calling read_to_end without a take limit would allow allocation to grow with the entire file before checking its size. A check after unbounded ingestion does not enforce a memory-ingestion limit. The decoder also checks size because it is a public boundary that callers can use independently of File.

Convert the retained bytes to UTF-8 only after the read succeeds and the size is acceptable. A failed conversion means the file violates the format, not that invalid bytes should be silently removed. File::open and Read failures are wrapped as Error::Io, retaining the original error as a source. That source chain lets callers inspect the underlying failure while a display message supplies domain context. Stringifying every error too early would throw away that structure.

Guided checkpoint: replacing a complete file

The save method encodes into memory, verifies its output limit, and creates a sibling temporary file using create_new. That option refuses to overwrite an existing temporary path. It writes all bytes, synchronizes the temporary file, closes it, and renames it onto the destination. On an error after temporary creation, it attempts to remove its own temporary file. A reader should not observe a half-written replacement produced by this process's ordinary write sequence.

The guarantee has limits. The implementation has no multi-process locking, and two writers can lose each other's updates. It does not fsync the containing directory, so do not claim a full power-loss durability guarantee. Rename replacement behavior and failures depend on the filesystem and operating system; test the target platform. A stale same-process-name temporary file causes a reported error rather than unsafe overwriting. These are concrete design limits, not generic warnings attached to every program.

Intentional mistake: truncate before you know you can finish

Sketch the simpler implementation File::create(destination), then write_all. Opening with truncation can erase the old contents before the new bytes have been fully written. If a later write fails, the old complete file is gone. The temporary-file protocol changes that ordering. Do not simulate disk-full failures by filling your machine. Instead, reason about the sequence and use a controlled failing writer abstraction in an extension if you want fault-injection tests.

Also avoid printing “saved” before save returns successfully. Process messages are part of the observable contract. The reference prints added only after persistence succeeds, so a success message does not claim an uncompleted storage operation. The in-memory object may have changed before save fails, but the short-lived CLI exits on that error; a long-lived UI would need an explicit unsaved-state policy.

Playbook: an existing journal appears empty

Observation: a learner program lists zero tasks when opening a protected or invalid path. Hypothesis A: decoding a valid empty journal is correct. Hypothesis B: an error was converted to an empty default by unwrap_or_default. Distinguishing experiment: load a known malformed file whose bytes are fixed and inspect the Result directly in a test. Expected reference result: Err. If the learner returns Ok(empty), the “valid empty file” explanation is disproven without relying on platform-specific permission behavior.

Trace the first place an error becomes success. The smallest fix is to special-case NotFound at the open boundary and propagate other errors, not to add retries everywhere. Record which failure you actually reproduced and which platform cases remain untested. Ask AI for the failure sequence under each proposed save protocol, then challenge it to identify what rename and sync_all do not guarantee together in this implementation.

A failed acknowledgement does not undo a save

The CLI saves an added task before writing added ID. Both output writing and its final flush are fallible, so a closed pipe exits with an I/O error instead of panicking. The save may already have succeeded. The output regression adds one task with stdout connected to a pipe whose read end is closed, observes failure, then reloads exactly one saved task. Repeating add blindly would create another task; inspect the journal after an uncertain acknowledgement. This is a local example of separating state change from delivery of its report, not a claim that the file format supports distributed idempotency.

When you get stuck: independent work and tiered help

Add a command that validates a journal without saving it. Return a nonzero exit for corrupted contents and preserve the file byte-for-byte. Next design, without claiming to implement it, how two simultaneous writers would coordinate. Name the lost-update scenario explicitly: each reads the same old state, each adds a different task, and the later save replaces the earlier update. A temporary filename alone does not solve this.

Hint 1: choose the next observation

inspect Result at each IO boundary before changing the parser.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

compare missing-path handling with malformed-file handling in the integration test.

Worked solution

match File::open, return an empty model only for NotFound, then propagate bounded-read and decoding errors with ?. A review request should include the initial file bytes, exact command, final bytes, and the first error observed. Avoid sharing personal journal contents when a three-row synthetic fixture reproduces the issue.

Review and mastery

The recommended design isolates pure parsing from file access and presentation, then tests each relevant boundary. A temporary replacement protocol is appropriate for this documented single-writer local journal. A transactional database is a meaningful alternative when concurrent writers, crash recovery, richer queries, or durable identity history become actual requirements. It adds operational and schema concerns, so it should be selected for those guarantees rather than as a status symbol.

Engineering decisions and evidence

Requirements and invariants

Tasks have private validated titles, nonzero unique current-file IDs, and one of two statuses. A failed domain validation leaves state unchanged. The versioned decoder rejects unknown headers, malformed rows, duplicate IDs, oversized files, and invalid UTF-8. Missing files start a journal; other load failures are retained.

Chosen design and concrete habits

Journal methods own state transitions, borrowed getters avoid incidental copies, and a pure decoder separates format checks from filesystem effects. load caps ingestion before decoding. save writes and syncs a sibling temporary file before rename, and success messages occur only after save returns. IO errors preserve their source. The String formatting expect is an internal infallibility assertion, not a policy for routine disk errors.

Meaningful alternative and evolution threshold

A database or explicit locking protocol is required when multiple writers must coordinate or stronger crash-recovery guarantees matter. The current rename sequence has no parent-directory fsync and no concurrency control. IDs may be reused after removing the current maximum; permanent external identity or audit history would justify a persisted monotonic allocator or event log. These changes follow concrete requirements.

Actual checks and remaining uncertainty

Native state-transition, malformed-format, fixture, filesystem replacement, and documentation tests passed in verification/native-tests.log and passed again in verification/patch001-foundations-tests.log after the patch audit. Tests show corrupt input is retained and valid state reloads on the tested local filesystem. They do not simulate power failure, all permission modes, or simultaneous writers. Independent review remains pending.

title: Stream logs with bounded lines and honest accounting
summary: Stream, validate, search and summarize Unicode log records with explicit memory and work budgets.
objectives: Separate streaming from bounded buffering
Drain oversized records and resume at the next boundary
Prove accounting relationships over accepted and rejected lines
Perform case-sensitive UTF-8 literal search without retaining matches
Separate a large total-byte work budget from bounded line memory
Propagate partial output failures and preserve all-record accounting
body:
Purpose: one bad line must not control memory

A log analyzer may process a large file without needing all of it at once. Streaming means you consume a sequence incrementally. Bounded buffering is the stronger claim that retained data cannot grow beyond an explicit limit. Using BufRead::lines streams across records, but a single line can still be arbitrarily long. A file containing ten million bytes before its first newline defeats the casual claim that “one line at a time” guarantees small memory use.

The CLI limits each line to 4096 bytes before the LF delimiter and defaults to a 64 MiB total-input budget. An explicit --max-bytes N raises that budget for larger files without raising the retained-line limit. Oversized lines are drained and counted separately. Invalid UTF-8 or malformed records are counted as malformed. IO failures and total-input exhaustion return an error rather than a misleading partial report. These are policy decisions: some applications need fail-fast ingestion, others tolerant ingestion with rejection counts. The chosen policy must be visible in both types and output.

Prediction before reading the implementation

The sample fixture contains five lines: two INFO records, one WARN, one malformed row, and one ERROR. Predict report totals before running it. Expected: lines=5, valid=4, malformed=1, oversized=0, info=2, warnings=1, errors=1. A blank physical line counts as a malformed line; a missing final newline does not erase a final nonempty record. CRLF is accepted by stripping one carriage return before parsing, although the byte bound counts that carriage return.

mise exec -- cargo run -p log-detective -- reference/p03-logs/fixtures/sample.log
mise exec -- cargo test -p log-detective tiny_buffers_and_final_line
mise exec -- cargo test -p log-detective drain_oversized_then_recover
mise exec -- cargo run -p log-detective -- --contains api reference/p03-logs/fixtures/sample.log

For the final command, predict two emitted records: timestamps 100 and 102. Search matches the complete valid line, including its service field. Stdout contains only the matching records; stderr contains the same all-record summary plus matched=2. Without a query, the existing summary remains on stdout. Zero matches is still a successful scan. Working directory for these commands: projects/.

The record grammar is intentionally strict: unsigned timestamp, known uppercase level, an ASCII service identifier, then a nonempty message. Single spaces separate the first fields; remaining spaces belong to the message. There is no timezone conversion or free-form date parsing. A timestamp is an integer supplied by the log producer. Decide what a field means before choosing a parser; a sophisticated parser cannot repair an unspecified format.

Guided checkpoint: observe, retain, consume

Read read_bounded as a small state machine. fill_buf exposes available bytes borrowed from the reader. Search that slice for LF. Decide how many bytes belong to this chunk and whether retaining them would exceed the line limit. Copy only while the line remains within the bound. If it becomes oversized, clear the retained data, set the oversized flag, and keep consuming until LF or end-of-input. consume advances the reader after the borrowed buffer has been inspected.

The distinction between retained bytes and consumed bytes is the core of the algorithm. Once a line is oversized, refusing to consume further bytes would revisit the same chunk forever. Returning immediately without draining would interpret the tail of the oversized line as a new record. The flag remembers that the current physical line has already been rejected while the reader moves to the next trustworthy boundary.

After a bounded line is complete, convert its bytes to UTF-8 and parse a borrowed Record. Increment exactly one of valid, malformed, or oversized for each counted line. For valid records, increment exactly one severity count. These relationships become testable invariants: lines equals valid plus malformed plus oversized, and valid equals info plus warnings plus errors. Accounting invariants catch missing branches even when individual example outputs look plausible.

Guided search increment: emit views before reusing storage

Literal search asks whether a sequence of characters appears inside a valid line. It does not interpret regular-expression symbols: a period matches a period. Add the SearchReport type after Report in src/lib.rs; it keeps the existing complete summary and a separate matched counter. Refactor the old loop into scan, taking an optional borrowed query and a Write destination. Keep analyze as a wrapper that supplies no query and io::sink(), a standard writer that discards bytes. This preserves the original analysis behavior while both entry points share one tested framing loop. The exact complete functions are in the source inclusion above; no omitted helper is needed.

In the valid-record branch, update the all-record counters first. Only then test text.contains(query). The if let pattern obtains a query and valid text, and its following && condition requires a match. A matching line is borrowed only until write_all finishes, so the next loop may safely reuse its byte buffer. W: Write means that the supplied value supports writing bytes, just as R: BufRead requires buffered reading. You will learn how these trait bounds support reusable libraries in Stage 2; here their concrete benefit is testing with a byte vector, a discard writer and a writer that deliberately fails. No collection of matching strings is needed.

Rust 1.99 str::contains accepts a string pattern and finds a matching string slice. Searching validated UTF-8 avoids slicing through a character. The policy is case-sensitive and performs no Unicode normalization: café with a precomposed é differs from cafe followed by a combining accent. A query must contain 1–4096 UTF-8 bytes and no control characters. Invalid and oversized records never reach the search writer. Valid messages already reject controls, including escape characters, but the tool does not redact secrets.

Write::write_all repeats partial writes until all bytes are written or an error occurs. A single write call may legally accept fewer bytes than requested. Write the normalized record, then LF. CRLF input becomes LF output, and an unterminated final record gains LF: this is normalized record output, not a raw byte-for-byte copy. If the reader, total budget or writer fails after several matches, those matches may already be visible. Return the error and treat that output as an incomplete prefix. Streaming publication is not an atomic transaction.

Replace the learner CLI's single-path argument handling in src/main.rs with the complete implementation below. args_os preserves native file paths. Only the query and positive decimal byte budget require Unicode text. Options precede the path; -- ends option recognition for a path beginning with a dash. The command line keeps its 4096-byte line bound. File reads use an explicit 8192-byte BufReader. The final flush must succeed before the CLI prints a success summary; a broken pipe is a failed scan with exit status 1. Failure to write a diagnostic cannot repair the original error, so main deliberately ignores that second error while retaining a failing exit status.

mise exec -- cargo test -p log-detective --locked
mise exec -- cargo run -p log-detective -- --contains unavailable --max-bytes 10737418240 /path/to/large.log

The second command is a usage template: substitute an existing file. Its 10 GiB work budget is an explicit choice, not a 10 GiB allocation. All discarded bytes and line terminators count. A buffered reader may prefetch into its bounded buffer before the scanner detects budget exhaustion. The scanner stores one bounded line, a bounded query and a fixed number of counters. It therefore supports files larger than available memory, provided the reader and output destination also stream. The supplied generated-reader test exercises 67,109,888 bytes using one 1 KiB repeated record and a 257-byte reader buffer; it does not claim that this amount exceeded this computer's physical RAM or that RSS was measured.

Playbook: a visually identical word does not match

Observation: café matches a record copied from one producer but not a visually identical record from another. Hypothesis A: a two-byte é was split at a reader boundary. Hypothesis B: the producers used different Unicode sequences. First run the same bytes with capacities 1 and 32. The reference produces identical counts, weakening A. Then inspect the Rust string escapes in unicode_literal_matching_is_independent_of_chunk_boundaries: one contains a precomposed é and the other an e followed by a combining accent. Comparing those exact sequences supports B. The smallest sound action is to honor the declared literal contract and explain the difference. Adding normalization is a new requirement, not a buffering fix.

Predict a second failure: a writer accepts five bytes, then returns BrokenPipe. The output_failure_returns_error_instead_of_successful_report test checks that this is an error, not a successful one-match report. The companion read-error test deliberately observes a complete emitted prefix followed by an input failure. Read those tests before deciding whether a downstream pipeline may trust partial output. Preserve the exit status along with the data.

Intentional mistake: returning at the size boundary

In a learner copy, return Oversized as soon as retained bytes would cross the limit. With a long line followed by a valid record, the next call begins halfway through the rejected line. Your report may count several malformed fragments or lose the real next record. The fix is not to increase the default limit until the test passes. Restore the record-boundary protocol: drain the rejected physical line, then report one oversized record.

A separate mistake is calling read_to_string on the entire file and then iterating its lines. That can produce correct totals for small fixtures while violating the memory contract. Tests should exercise small reader buffer capacities, long lines, invalid bytes, and a final unterminated line. Memory claims also require code-level reasoning about allocation and retention; output equality alone cannot prove a bound.

Playbook: totals change with buffer size

Observation: the same bytes produce different counts when BufReader capacity changes from 1 to 4096. Hypothesis A: the record grammar depends on chunk boundaries. Hypothesis B: the implementation accidentally treats buffer chunks as complete lines. A distinguishing experiment uses a two-line fixed input and iterates capacities 1 through 32. Expected reference result: identical totals for every capacity. The grammar is defined by newline boundaries, so capacity-dependent results disprove a correct chunk-independent implementation.

Now inspect where a return occurs before LF. The experiment narrows the issue to buffering state, not timestamps or severity matching. Change only the chunk-handling logic, then rerun both the capacity sweep and malformed-input fixtures. Ask AI to draw the state transitions for “within limit,” “oversized but draining,” and “end of record.” Reject a proposed repair that simply calls lines(), because it abandons the explicit memory bound under investigation.

Reconstruct the complete early checkpoint

This complete early checkpoint isolates bounded LF byte-line framing and draining. It deliberately precedes CRLF normalization, UTF-8 log grammar and report accounting. The checkpoint contract and source are separately preserved. From the course root, run:

python3 scripts/start-checkpoint.py p03 01-bounded-lines
cd learner-work/checkpoints/p03-logs/01-bounded-lines
mise exec -- cargo test
mise exec -- cargo run

The helper refuses an existing destination; choose a new explicit destination if you already have work there. This is a complete guided comparison checkpoint, not evidence that you independently implemented the project. Make predictions, inspect each boundary test, then carry the next requirement into your own source. A separately named final checkpoint reconstructs the current complete reference without pretending it is this earlier milestone. Exact reconstruction and test commands are recorded in the author check log.

When you get stuck: independent work and tiered help

Add an optional severity filter while preserving total accounting. Decide whether valid means all syntactically valid rows or only matching rows; use a separate matched counter if both are useful. Then add a test where an oversized line appears between two valid ERROR records. Explain whether the total-input limit includes discarded bytes; in this reference it does, preventing unlimited processing of rejected data. Keep that rule when extending the analyzer.

Hint 1: choose the next observation

write down the state carried between fill_buf calls.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

test a reader with capacity 1 so every boundary becomes visible.

Worked solution

maintain a boolean oversized flag, stop appending after the limit, continue consume calls until newline, then increment oversized exactly once. A useful review request supplies raw input bytes, buffer capacity, limits, and expected counters. Do not paste megabytes of logs when a 30-byte fixture reproduces the boundary error.

Review, limits, and mastery

The recommended analyzer bounds retained bytes and total consumed input at the point of ingestion, with explicit rejected-record accounting. A whole-file immutable buffer would simplify borrowed long-lived views but would require a different, small-file resource contract. Reader buffering still adds memory beyond the retained line Vec; the caller controls that buffer. The total byte limit bounds processed input, not elapsed wall-clock time for a slow blocking reader.

Mastery means explaining why a huge line cannot make the retained line buffer grow without limit, why analysis resumes correctly afterward, and why counters remain consistent. The deterministic buffer-size sweep is finite evidence over selected inputs, not a proof for all streams. Pair it with an argument about every state transition, the injected read/write failure tests and a record of still-untested operating-system conditions. This is the first course project where the resource contract deserves as much attention as the numeric output.

Engineering decisions and evidence

Requirements and invariants

Retain at most the configured line payload, count each physical line once, drain oversized lines, propagate read/write failures and reject input beyond its total-byte budget. Summary categories partition all counted lines; severity counters partition valid records. Search matches are a subset of valid records. UTF-8 views never outlive the stable current line. Output already written may remain when a later operation fails.

Chosen design and concrete habits

The shared scan state machine uses fill_buf and consume. analyze supplies a discard writer with no query; search supplies a bounded literal and the caller's writer. Fixed counters avoid a service-name map with attacker-controlled cardinality. A parsed Record borrows its fields for immediate accounting, while str::contains searches the whole validated line without byte indexing. write_all handles short writes and returns ordinary failures. The CLI uses args_os for native paths, validates textual options, owns stdout flushing and reports success only after that flush.

Meaningful alternative and evolution threshold
