A whole-file buffer is suitable only under a separately justified small-file memory contract. Raising --max-bytes changes the allowed work, not the retained-line bound. Regular expressions, normalized or case-insensitive Unicode matching require explicit semantics and may justify a maintained library. Per-service aggregation needs bounded cardinality. A blocking byte budget does not provide a wall-clock deadline. Atomic output publication would require a separate temporary-file and replacement contract; this tool deliberately exposes streaming prefix-on-error behavior.

Actual checks and remaining uncertainty

The search follow-up records unit, CLI, integration and documentation tests, strict Clippy, all-target checking and formatting. A generated reader processed 67,109,888 bytes from one 1 KiB record through a 257-byte reader, with all 65,537 records counted and matched. Unicode, partial output failures, a read error after emitted output, Interrupted retry and budget boundaries are tested. This supports the declared stream contract; it is not an RSS benchmark or proof for every input. Reader/writer storage and allocator overhead add memory. Independent review remains pending.

title: Traits as required capabilities, not decoration
summary: Use generic readers and formatters to separate behavior from concrete storage and presentation choices.
objectives: Read a trait bound as an explicit capability requirement
Choose static dispatch when one generic implementation suffices
Test behavior through injected inputs instead of global state
body:
Purpose: reuse the algorithm without hiding its needs

The log analyzer accepts any type implementing BufRead. A file-backed BufReader, locked standard input, and a byte slice can all supply buffered bytes. The algorithm does not need to know which one it received; it needs the capability to inspect buffered data and consume it. A trait names that capability. A generic bound tells the compiler and the reader which operations a function is permitted to use on an otherwise unspecified type.

This is a better starting model than “traits are interfaces” alone. The important question is what behavior the function requires and who supplies it. analyze<R: BufRead> states a concrete requirement. It is not a promise that every possible input source is nonblocking, trustworthy, or equally fast. A capability boundary should be narrow enough to support reuse but honest about the remaining behavioral assumptions.

Prediction: same data, different source

Predict whether analyze receives the same report from a byte slice and from a BufReader around Cursor when both contain identical bytes. Expected: yes. Neither source changes the record grammar. The tiny-buffer tests already exercise this idea. They demonstrate how a generic API creates useful test seams: you can change the source implementation without changing the parser or introducing files solely for a unit test.

mise exec -- cargo test -p log-detective accounting_property_across_buffer_sizes
mise exec -- cargo test -p typed-config later_layers_win_before_validation

In the configuration project, Layer::environment accepts an iterator of name/value pairs. Tests pass a small array, while main supplies actual process environment pairs. This is dependency injection in plain Rust: make input explicit in a parameter. It avoids mutating global process environment during tests, which would complicate parallel execution and introduce cross-test interference. You do not need a container framework to get the important benefit.

Guided checkpoint: read the bounds literally

Read the environment signature. IntoIterator means the supplied value can produce an iterator. The item is a pair. Each name and value supports AsRef<str>, so the function can borrow text without insisting on one concrete owned-string type. Follow one iteration and identify when a borrowed name is matched and when a recognized value is copied into the layer's owned map. The bounds support the operations the body actually performs.

Now read Display for CalcError or ConfigError. Display describes user-facing formatting; Debug is intended for developer-oriented inspection. Deriving Debug is convenient only when every displayed field is safe and appropriate to expose. Secret deliberately implements Debug to print a redaction marker. Choosing a trait implementation is part of observable program behavior, not a cosmetic annotation. A diagnostic path can leak sensitive text just as a normal output path can.

Intentional compiler mistake

The supplied 05-missing-trait.rs fixture defines fn render<T>(value: T) and tries to print it with {}. Predict the error before compiling: the body requires Display, but the signature promises no such capability. Adding T: std::fmt::Display is a sound repair because it states the real requirement. Replacing formatting with an unrelated conversion may only move the problem. Generic code must be valid for every type satisfying its declared bounds, not merely the type used by one call site today.

mise exec -- rustc --edition=2024 --emit=metadata --out-dir /tmp/rust-course-diagnostics 05-missing-trait.rs

Run that command from rust-course/exercises/foundations, where the fixture resides. Expected result is a nonzero exit including E0277. The command is intentionally outside the Cargo reference workspace. After you write a corrected scratch copy, compile it and explain why callers with non-Display types are now rejected at the boundary. The added bound narrows valid callers in exchange for a well-defined operation.

Static dispatch and deliberate restraint

A generic function is compiled for concrete types as needed. A trait object such as &mut dyn BufRead instead supports dynamic dispatch through a runtime interface. Both are useful; neither is automatically more idiomatic. This project uses a generic function because each call already has one concrete reader type and the implementation is straightforward. Introduce a trait object when you need heterogeneous values behind one runtime type, not merely because the word “abstraction” sounds desirable.

Do not create a custom trait with one method for every helper function. Traits pay for themselves when they describe a coherent capability, enable distinct implementations, or express a real generic relationship. Ordinary functions and structs are often clearer. In the config project, Layer is a concrete collection of text; making every layer source implement a custom repository trait would add ceremony without improving the current two test scenarios.

Playbook: a test passes alone and fails with others

Observation: configuration tests sometimes see another test's environment override. Hypothesis A: map iteration order changes precedence. Hypothesis B: tests share mutable process environment. A distinguishing experiment passes an explicit fixed array to Layer::environment and removes environment mutation from the test. Expected result: deterministic values regardless of neighboring tests. That disproves map order as the cause of this reproduction when the same merge order is retained and supports the shared-input explanation.

Keep the precedence logic unchanged during that experiment. If you reorder layers at the same time, you lose the ability to distinguish causes. Record the original global dependency and the new explicit input boundary. Ask AI to explain which dependency became injectable and which effects still occur in main. A sound explanation should not claim that a pure test proves operating-system environment encoding behavior.

When you get stuck: independent work and tiered help

Write a report function accepting impl std::io::Write and serialize the log counters into it. Test with a Vec<u8>, then call it with standard output. Add a controlled writer that returns an IO error after a chosen byte count and ensure the error is preserved. This connects a trait requirement to a concrete failure mode. Do not call flush automatically without deciding whether your function owns completion of the output stream.

Hint 1: choose the next observation

list the methods your function body calls on its parameter.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

find the trait that provides those methods and use only that bound.

Worked solution

fn write_report(mut output: impl Write, report: &Report) -> io::Result<()> can use writeln! and return its Result; a Vec<u8> then serves as an in-memory sink. Ask for a review of the smallest sufficient bound and error contract. More bounds do not necessarily mean a better abstraction.

Review and mastery evidence

The recommended functions accept explicit input through standard capabilities and keep process environment or filesystem access in main. This supplies useful test seams with a small API. Concrete parameters remain a valid choice when a function has exactly one meaningful representation; a trait object becomes useful when runtime heterogeneity is required. Choose the least complex interface that expresses the real capability and preserves errors.

title: Layer configuration, then validate the effective state
summary: Build a typed configuration boundary with deterministic precedence and redacted secrets.
objectives: Specify merge order separately from validation order
Represent validated values with constrained types
Prevent accidental secret exposure in formatting and errors
body:
Purpose: one effective configuration, one clear precedence

Applications often combine defaults, a configuration file, environment variables, and command-line overrides. Bugs arise when different parts of the program resolve precedence differently or parse the same raw text repeatedly. This project constructs one effective raw map, validates it once, and exposes a typed Config. Later code receives an IP address, a nonzero port, a Duration, a bounded connection count, and an optional Secret rather than a collection of unchecked strings.

The precedence is defaults, then file, then APP_* environment, then --set arguments. Later layers replace earlier values with the same recognized key. Structural checks occur within each layer: unknown keys and duplicates are rejected. Semantic validation occurs after merging. Therefore a higher-precedence valid port can repair a lower-precedence invalid port value. This policy is intentional; another application might validate every layer independently to catch stale mistakes, but that would yield different behavior.

Predict before running a layered case

The fixture sets port=9000. Predict the result when the environment sets APP_PORT=9001 and the command line sets port=9002. Expected: 9002. Then predict a file containing port=bad with a command-line port=9002. The reference accepts the effective value because validation occurs after resolution. Removing the command-line repair exposes the invalid final value and produces a configuration error.

mise exec -- cargo run -p typed-config -- --file reference/p04-config/fixtures/app.conf --set port=9002
mise exec -- cargo test -p typed-config later_layers_win_before_validation
mise exec -- cargo test -p typed-config --test cli

The first command's output also depends on recognized APP_* values already present in your shell. The integration test controls the child process environment, then sets known values and verifies command-line precedence. That controlled setup is stronger evidence for precedence than a terminal run whose environment you never recorded. Avoid placing real secrets in commands while practicing; synthetic markers are sufficient to test redaction.

Guided checkpoint: raw input becomes constrained state

Layer::parse accepts strict key=value lines, blank lines, and full-line comments beginning with #. It trims surrounding whitespace from keys and values. It does not implement inline comments or quoting. A token containing # therefore retains that character rather than silently losing a suffix. Clear grammar prevents configuration from becoming a collection of surprising heuristics. File size and individual value limits bound accepted text before it becomes stored state.

Resolve merges owned maps and validates the effective values. NonZeroU16 makes port zero unrepresentable in the resulting Config. IpAddr distinguishes actual IP addresses from arbitrary host strings; localhost is intentionally not a valid input here. Duration expresses seconds as time rather than a bare number that callers might interpret as milliseconds. The connection limit remains u16, protected by private fields and constructor validation. Types and privacy work together; not every useful constraint has a built-in standard-library type.

A missing token becomes None. An explicitly present empty token is invalid, not equivalent to missing. That distinction matters when an override accidentally erases a required value. The current reference makes tokens optional; do not infer authentication policy from the existence of a token field. It is a configuration teaching model, not a complete security system.

Redaction is observable behavior

Secret wraps a String and implements Debug with a fixed redaction marker. Config can then derive Debug without printing the token's contents. Layer's Debug prints keys only, because raw layers may contain invalid or unclassified sensitive values. ConfigError identifies a key and a problem without echoing the input value. These choices reduce accidental disclosure through routine debugging and error presentation.

The wrapper does not encrypt memory, zeroize allocations, or prevent a caller from deliberately invoking expose and printing the returned text. Its purpose is to make ordinary formatting safe by default and intentional access visible in code review. Do not claim more. The tests search output for a synthetic marker and verify redaction in both library formatting and a launched CLI process. They are behavioral evidence for those paths, not a guarantee about every future log statement.

Intentional mistake and playbook investigation

Introduce a learner bug by reversing the layer iteration order. Observation: the file value wins over a command-line override. Hypothesis A: the CLI parser failed to capture --set. Hypothesis B: the merge applies high-precedence values too early and then overwrites them. Distinguishing experiment: call Config::resolve directly with two layers setting different ports, then reverse just their order. Expected reference behavior: the second layer wins in each case. If the learner result follows the first layer instead, the CLI hypothesis is disproven for the direct reproduction.

The smallest fix belongs in merge ordering, followed by regression tests that preserve unrelated keys from lower layers. Do not “fix” it by special-casing port after validation; that creates a second precedence system. Record the input order, effective result, and expected result. Ask AI to propose a counterexample to the corrected merge, especially a layer that overrides one key while leaving another untouched. Evaluate the counterexample before accepting any generalized claim.

Reconstruct the complete early checkpoint

This complete early checkpoint resolves only optional port layers and validates the final value. Files, process environment, other fields and secret redaction are later boundaries. The checkpoint contract and source are separately preserved. From the course root, run:

python3 scripts/start-checkpoint.py p04 01-effective-port
cd learner-work/checkpoints/p04-config/01-effective-port
mise exec -- cargo test
mise exec -- cargo run

The helper refuses an existing destination; choose a new explicit destination if you already have work there. This is a complete guided comparison checkpoint, not evidence that you independently implemented the project. Make predictions, inspect each boundary test, then carry the next requirement into your own source. A separately named final checkpoint reconstructs the current complete reference without pretending it is this earlier milestone. Exact reconstruction and test commands are recorded in the author check log.

Redacted output can still fail

The CLI writes the already-redacted Debug representation through fallible writeln! and flush. A closed output pipe returns failure, and a second failure on stderr is handled as a best-effort diagnostic rather than a panic. These output checks preserve secret redaction; they do not make a terminal a confidential destination. The child-process regression closes the only pipe reader before execution to force the relevant I/O failure deterministically.

When you get stuck: independent work and tiered help

Add a validated log_level key with a closed enum. Support exactly info, warn, and error; reject other spellings unless you explicitly choose normalization. Preserve default/file/environment/CLI precedence and ensure Debug still redacts the token. Add one test for an invalid lower layer repaired by a valid upper layer, one for an invalid effective value, and one showing an unrelated lower-layer timeout survives a port override.

Hint 1: choose the next observation

inspect the raw merged value before changing type conversion, using only non-secret synthetic inputs.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

distinguish duplicate keys within one layer from the same key across layers.

Worked solution

extend raw values in declared precedence order, then parse each final field into a validated type and construct Config only after all fields pass. A concise review request includes your precedence rule, one two-layer counterexample, and the new enum's accepted spellings. Ask an AI reviewer to search for secret exposure in errors as well as in Debug.

Recommended design and alternatives

The recommended design resolves precedence once and validates once, so application code receives stable typed values. A concrete map and constructor are appropriate for five keys and four sources. A configuration library can help when nested schemas, multiple file syntaxes, or source-location diagnostics become requirements. Your precedence, accepted values, and redaction policy remain explicit requirements even when syntax parsing moves into a dependency.

Mastery means predicting the effective configuration for three layers without running the program, explaining why zero cannot appear in a constructed port, and demonstrating that a token marker does not appear in tested output paths. State the limits: environment bytes that are not Unicode are skipped by this simple CLI adapter, and the secret wrapper does not provide memory erasure. A complete design note names such boundaries so a future production adaptation can decide which ones must change.

Engineering decisions and evidence

Requirements and invariants

Resolve defaults < file < environment < command line, reject unknown or duplicate keys within one layer, then validate effective values. Constructed ports are nonzero, timeouts and connection counts are bounded, hosts are IP addresses, and ordinary formatting/errors do not expose tokens. An explicitly empty token differs from an absent token.

Chosen design and concrete habits

Raw Layer and validated Config are separate types. Layer::environment takes injected pairs for parallel-safe tests instead of mutating process environment. Private fields and NonZeroU16 protect accepted state. Secret implements redacted Debug; errors identify keys and rules without echoing input. Normal parsing and IO failures use Result from the first recommended checkpoint, including documentation examples.

Meaningful alternative and evolution threshold

Validating each raw layer before merge is defensible when stale invalid configuration must be rejected even if overridden; it is a different policy and needs different tests. A schema library becomes useful for nested structures and source-location diagnostics. Required credentials, zeroization, or a real secret provider require explicit new guarantees; this redaction wrapper does not encrypt or erase memory.

Actual checks and remaining uncertainty

Native precedence, boundary, redaction, controlled-child-environment CLI, and documentation tests passed in verification/native-tests.log and passed again in verification/patch001-foundations-tests.log after the patch audit. Tested output paths omit synthetic token markers. The CLI skips non-Unicode environment pairs, and future hand-written logging can still expose values deliberately. Independent review remains pending.

title: Borrowed views: describe the owner instead of fighting annotations
summary: Explain Record lifetimes and choose when a view must become owned data.
objectives: Connect returned slices to the input that owns their bytes
Distinguish lifetime relationships from extending storage
Design streaming aggregation that does not retain stale line views
body:
Purpose: parse text without copying every field

The log parser returns a Record containing a numeric timestamp, a copied Level, and borrowed service and message slices. Those slices point into the input line. This is efficient and easy to reason about while the analyzer uses the record immediately, updates counters, and then reuses its line buffer. The lifetime question becomes concrete: how long may a Record view remain valid relative to the String or byte buffer that owns its text?

A lifetime annotation describes a relationship between references. It does not allocate memory, delay destruction, or extend the life of a local variable. Record<'a> says that its borrowed fields remain valid for an appropriate lifetime 'a. parse_record(input: &str) -> Result<Record<'_>, ...> connects the returned view to the borrowed input through elision. The compiler checks that callers do not keep using the view after its backing text can change or disappear.

Prediction: which value must survive?

Predict whether a function can create a local String, parse a borrowed Record from it, and return that Record. Expected: no, because the String is dropped at the function's end while the returned fields would refer to its former allocation. Adding 'static to the return type cannot repair the ownership problem. A static string literal can support a static view; a String constructed inside the function does not become static by declaration.

mise exec -- cargo test -p log-detective

From rust-course/exercises/foundations, also run the deliberately failing local-reference example. Expected result: a nonzero exit with E0515. Write down the owner that disappears and the reference that would escape before reading the hint. The simplified function in that fixture returns &str rather than Record, but the underlying relationship is the same.

mise exec -- rustc --edition=2024 --emit=metadata --out-dir /tmp/rust-course-diagnostics 03-local-reference.rs

Guided checkpoint: follow one borrowed record

Read parse_record and mark where splitn returns slices of its input. Parsing timestamp produces an owned u64 value. Matching level produces a small owned enum. service and message remain slices into the original line. No collection of newly allocated strings is required for these fields. Then read analyze: the record is consumed for counting within the current loop iteration, and no borrowed field is stored in Report. The next read may clear and reuse the line buffer only after those views are no longer needed.

This local-use pattern is a common way to make borrowing simple. Do not retain references merely to avoid all allocations. If the feature requires a list of error messages after the file has been read, those selected messages need storage that survives the reused buffer. One reasonable design allocates owned Strings only for retained errors. Another stores offsets into an immutable whole-file buffer, but that changes the memory contract. The correct ownership model follows the feature's retention requirements.

An explicit two-input relationship

Consider a helper that returns the longer of two borrowed service names. If it can return either argument, both inputs and the output need a common lifetime relationship, often written fn longer<'a>(left: &'a str, right: &'a str) -> &'a str. This does not force the original Strings to live equally long. It requires the returned view to be used within a period for which the selected inputs can support the relationship. The caller may use a shorter overlap even if one owner lives much longer.

If the function always returns left, a second independent lifetime or an elided right input can express that weaker relationship. This distinction matters: annotations should state the actual source of returned references, not tie everything together by habit. A compiler suggestion can make code compile while imposing a unnecessarily restrictive API. Read the function body and the caller's need before accepting a proposed lifetime signature.

Intentional mistake: collect views from a reusable buffer

In a learner analyzer, try pushing record.message into Vec<&str> while repeatedly clearing and refilling the same String. The desired Vec claims that all messages remain available, while the storage strategy keeps only one mutable line. The borrow checker exposes that contradiction. The fix is not a longer annotation or an unsafe pointer. Either own each retained message, retain the original backing storage, or change the output to aggregate information that does not need old text.

Cloning the entire file would technically provide durable storage but violate the streaming project's resource goal. Allocating every message may also violate the intended bounded report unless you impose a retention limit. A safe design must satisfy both ownership and resource requirements. Memory safety alone does not imply acceptable memory growth. State a maximum number or total bytes of retained examples if your report gains sample messages.

Playbook: the compiler rejects collected messages

Observation: the analyzer compiles when it counts errors but fails when it stores borrowed messages across iterations. Hypothesis A: Record<'_> needs a different spelling of its lifetime. Hypothesis B: retained views outlive the reusable line buffer's stable contents. Distinguishing experiment: replace the stored &str with an owned String for one selected message while leaving parsing unchanged. Expected result: the ownership conflict disappears. This supports B and disproves a missing-annotation explanation for this design.

That experiment does not automatically justify unbounded retention. Follow it with a second design question: what is the maximum retained data? Record both conclusions separately. Ask AI to draw owner/view lifetimes for the original and revised design, then ask for a counterexample to its memory-bound claim. A useful answer should mention the number of errors, not merely say that cloning is safe.

When you get stuck: independent work and tiered help

Extend Report with at most three owned example messages from malformed UTF-8-valid lines, truncating each example at a safe UTF-8 boundary under a documented byte limit. Decide how invalid UTF-8 input is represented without inventing text that was not present. Test a multibyte character at the truncation boundary. Your extension changes retention deliberately while keeping a bounded amount of additional memory. The supplied reference remains counters-only, so keep this experiment in your learner workspace.

Hint 1: choose the next observation

identify the owner of every returned slice and its last mutation.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

ask whether the caller needs a view or an independent snapshot.

Worked solution for selected valid text

use message.to_owned() only when retaining it, enforce a maximum retained count, and discard the temporary borrowed Record before reading again. For truncation, retreat to a char boundary rather than slicing at an arbitrary byte. A review request should include the ownership diagram and the proposed bound, not just the lifetime error text.

Review and mastery

The recommended approach chooses storage according to retention requirements, then describes the resulting reference relationships. Borrowed records are appropriate for immediate aggregation; bounded owned samples are appropriate when selected messages must survive buffer reuse. Elided lifetimes keep an unambiguous single-input relationship concise, while explicit annotations communicate relationships involving multiple possible input owners. Neither representation replaces the need to account for retained memory.

Mastery means explaining why parse_record can return borrowed fields, why a local-owner function cannot, and how to retain a small bounded sample without stale references. Compilation is evidence for safe-reference validity, while tests verify field parsing and retention policy. Neither establishes a benchmark advantage over owned strings. If you claim a performance benefit, measure realistic workloads separately rather than inferring speed from the absence of one visible clone.

title: Parse expressions with precedence, byte spans, and limits
summary: Build a lexer and a precedence parser whose errors identify the exact input region.
objectives: Separate lexical tokens from recursive syntax
Implement left associativity with binding thresholds
Preserve UTF-8 byte spans and bound recursive work
body:
Purpose: turn a string into a structure with meaning

The calculator accepted exactly one operator. The expression language accepts combinations such as 2 + 3 * 4 and (2 + 3) * 4. Reading characters from left to right and applying operations immediately cannot represent precedence correctly. A parser builds an abstract syntax tree, or AST, that makes grouping explicit. Evaluation later follows that structure. This separation lets you test whether the expression means the right thing independently of whether its arithmetic fits in i64.

The language supports nonnegative i64 literals, unary minus, parentheses, and four binary operators. Multiplication and division bind more tightly than addition and subtraction. Binary operators associate left, so 20 - 5 - 3 means (20 - 5) - 3. Unary minus binds more tightly than multiplication. There is no unary plus, floating-point syntax, identifier, assignment, or implicit multiplication. A grammar with explicit exclusions is easier to implement and review than one that guesses what every unfamiliar character might mean.

Prediction and a grammar trace

Predict these results and sketch a tree before running: 2 + 3 * 4 gives 14; (2 + 3) * 4 gives 20; 20 - 5 - 3 gives 12; -3 * -2 gives 6. The tree for the first has addition at its root and multiplication as its right child. The parenthesized version has multiplication at the root and addition inside its left subtree. The difference is structure, not a different evaluation rule for the same tree.

mise exec -- cargo run -p expression-language -- '2 + 3 * 4'
mise exec -- cargo run -p expression-language -- '(2 + 3) * 4'
mise exec -- cargo test -p expression-language precedence_associativity_unary

Guided checkpoint: lex with source positions

The lexer scans bytes, skips ASCII whitespace, combines consecutive ASCII digits into one number token, and recognizes punctuation. Each token carries a half-open Span with start and end byte offsets. A range start..end includes start and excludes end, matching Rust slicing conventions. Unknown characters produce an error spanning the whole Unicode scalar value, so the four-byte crab symbol in 2 + 🦀 receives bytes 4..8 rather than a misleading one-byte range.

These offsets are bytes, not terminal columns or user-perceived character counts. The CLI prints the textual range and original source instead of drawing a caret at a byte count and pretending it is a display column. A richer editor integration would convert offsets with a documented line/column convention. Preserving precise source coordinates at lexing time is much easier than reconstructing them after tokens have lost their origin.

Guided checkpoint: precedence climbing

Parser::expression begins by parsing a prefix: number, unary minus, or a parenthesized expression. It then examines the following operator. If that operator's precedence meets the current minimum, it consumes the operator and parses the right-hand side with a higher minimum, precedence + 1. That increment makes operators of equal precedence stay for the outer loop, producing left associativity. Trace 20 - 5 - 3 and mark which recursive call is allowed to consume each minus.

Parentheses call expression with the lowest threshold and require a closing token afterward. Unary minus calls with a tighter threshold than multiplication. After the top-level expression returns, parse rejects any trailing token. Without that final check, input such as 1 2 could silently evaluate only the first number. Successful prefix parsing is not the same as successful whole-input parsing. Tests must include extra-token cases to enforce the boundary.

Resource limits are part of syntax handling

The parser limits source bytes to 4096, tokens to 512, recursive nesting to 64, and AST depth to 64. These are related but distinct protections. A long chain of additions can create a deep left-associated AST even when parentheses are shallow. Deep parentheses can create recursion without adding many AST nodes. Checking only one of these dimensions leaves another route to excessive stack use or work. The private Expr fields prevent external callers from constructing an arbitrarily deep tree that bypasses the parser's invariant.

An input can therefore be mathematically valid but rejected because it exceeds the resource contract. Return an explanatory error instead of panicking. The chosen limits are teaching defaults, not universal safe values for every platform. If you change them, test both acceptance just below the boundary and rejection above it, and reconsider recursive evaluation and destruction as well as parsing.

Intentional mistake and playbook investigation

Introduce a learner bug by parsing a binary right operand with the same minimum precedence instead of precedence + 1. Observation: 20 - 5 - 3 produces 18 rather than 12. Hypothesis A: subtraction arithmetic is wrong. Hypothesis B: equal-precedence operators grouped to the right. Distinguishing experiment: compare the unparenthesized input with both (20 - 5) - 3 and 20 - (5 - 3). Expected buggy result matches the right-grouped expression; a simple 20 - 5 still yields 15. This disproves basic subtraction as the cause and supports the grouping hypothesis.

The smallest fix is the binding threshold, followed by subtraction and division chain tests. Do not patch the evaluator to special-case consecutive subtraction. That would embed syntax repair in the wrong layer. Record the tree shape or a trace of token consumption as evidence. Ask AI to trace the parser calls with their minimum values; compare its trace against the actual code before accepting a claimed associativity fix.

Reconstruct the complete early checkpoint

This complete early checkpoint tokenizes nonnegative literals, plus and star with byte spans and resource bounds. Precedence parsing, unary signs, parentheses and evaluation belong to the later complete reference. The checkpoint contract and source are separately preserved. From the course root, run:

python3 scripts/start-checkpoint.py p05 01-token-spans
cd learner-work/checkpoints/p05-expressions/01-token-spans
mise exec -- cargo test
mise exec -- cargo run

The helper refuses an existing destination; choose a new explicit destination if you already have work there. This is a complete guided comparison checkpoint, not evidence that you independently implemented the project. Make predictions, inspect each boundary test, then carry the next requirement into your own source. A separately named final checkpoint reconstructs the current complete reference without pretending it is this earlier milestone. Exact reconstruction and test commands are recorded in the author check log.

When you get stuck: independent work and tiered help

Add a remainder operator to your learner language at multiplication's precedence. Specify left associativity and checked arithmetic behavior, including zero divisors. Add tests mixing remainder with multiplication and addition, not merely one isolated a % b case. Alternatively, add an AST pretty-printer that always parenthesizes binary expressions and verify that parsing its output preserves evaluation for your finite test domain. Keep source-span reporting for invalid input intact.

Hint 1: choose the next observation

test lexing and grouping separately before changing arithmetic.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

trace the current token index and minimum precedence on 8 / 4 / 2.

Worked solution

equal-precedence operators must remain in the outer loop for left associativity, so recurse on the right with precedence + 1. A review request should include the grammar rule, an ambiguous-looking expression, the intended tree, and the observed value. Ask a reviewer for one counterexample, not a wholesale parser rewrite.

Review and mastery evidence

The recommended parser uses tokens, preserved spans, and one explicit binding-threshold rule. This is a scope-appropriate implementation for four operators and unary negation. Separate recursive-descent functions can improve readability when grammar categories expand; a parser library may help with richer syntax or recovery. Choose those alternatives when the current representation makes actual language requirements difficult to state or verify.

Mastery means tracing token consumption, explaining left associativity, locating an error span in UTF-8 bytes, and showing how both a nested expression and a long flat chain are bounded. Passing the expression examples is evidence for those grammar cases. It does not prove every possible character sequence is handled correctly. The next lesson expands the evidence with arithmetic boundary tests and finite exhaustive properties while keeping those limits honest.

title: Evaluate safely and test properties without overstating them
summary: Connect recursive evaluation, checked arithmetic, deterministic property checks, and a completed project review.
objectives: Evaluate an AST in a specified order with checked operations
Distinguish example tests, finite properties, and proofs
Write a project review grounded in actual validation evidence
body:
Purpose: a correct tree still needs correct execution

A parser establishes structure. Evaluation gives that structure a result or a runtime domain error. The expression 8 / 0 is syntactically valid but cannot produce an integer under our arithmetic contract. The expression 1 2 is syntactically invalid and never reaches evaluation. Keeping those failures separate helps users and tests identify the boundary that rejected the input. Your finished project should make successful results, syntax failures, arithmetic failures, and resource-limit failures all deliberate outcomes.

The evaluator recursively visits Expr nodes. A number returns its stored i64. Unary negation evaluates its operand and uses checked_neg. A binary node evaluates its left child, then its right child, and applies the corresponding checked operation. This order is observable when more than one subtree could fail: the first error stops evaluation through ?. The language has no side effects, but error ordering still affects diagnostics. Do not assume that pure arithmetic means evaluation order is irrelevant to every user-visible result.

Prediction: where should the error point?

Predict the error for 8 / 0. Expected: division by zero at bytes 2..3, the slash. The full expression span remains available on the AST, while operator_span identifies the failing operation. For 9223372036854775807 + 1, expected failure is arithmetic overflow at the plus. For the literal 9223372036854775808, overflow happens during lexing before an AST is built. The same broad word “overflow” refers to different boundaries in these cases.

mise exec -- cargo run -p expression-language -- '8 / 0'
mise exec -- cargo run -p expression-language -- '9223372036854775807 + 1'
mise exec -- cargo test -p expression-language precise_error_spans
mise exec -- cargo test -p expression-language deterministic_exhaustive_small_integer_properties

A direct literal for i64::MIN is deliberately not supported by this grammar: unary minus applies to a nonnegative literal that must itself fit in i64. Write -9223372036854775807 - 1 to produce the minimum value. This limit is documented, not silently repaired in the lexer. If you later support the direct spelling, design how literal magnitudes and unary operations interact before changing parse types opportunistically.

Guided checkpoint: one recursive contract

Read Expr::evaluate and state its contract for each node variant. All successful values fit in i64. Division by zero gets its own message; checked_div still handles minimum divided by -1 as overflow. Negating the minimum similarly fails with checked_neg. The evaluator preserves the operator's source span when reporting arithmetic failure. The error payload is small and structured, allowing the CLI, tests, or a future editor to present it differently.

The parser has already enforced AST depth and keeps Expr fields private, so evaluation receives a bounded tree from the public parse API. That is a cross-layer invariant worth documenting: evaluation relies on construction constraints. A future public constructor or deserializer could invalidate the argument unless it also checks depth. A good review traces not only each function body but also every route by which its inputs can be constructed.

Examples, properties, and independent expectations

An example test asserts one known result, such as 2 + 3 * 4 = 14. A property states a relationship over a set of inputs, such as addition commutativity. The reference loops over small finite integer domains and checks expressions against direct Rust arithmetic that is safe within those chosen bounds. This is deterministic exhaustive checking over the specified domain. It is not randomized property testing, fuzzing, or a proof over all i64 values and all source strings.

The oracle matters. If a test computes its expected result using the same parser under test, the two sides can share the same defect. Comparing a parsed expression with a straightforward host-language expression on small bounded integers provides a more independent expectation. Even that oracle has assumptions: keep values small enough that ordinary arithmetic cannot overflow, and account for the same integer division semantics. Write those assumptions near the test rather than relying on intuition.

Intentional mistake: a property outside its preconditions

A tempting property is (a / b) * b == a for every nonzero b. Integer division truncates, so it fails whenever a is not divisible by b. For a=7 and b=2, the left side is 6. A failing test can expose a false test assumption instead of an implementation bug. Refine the property to cases with exact divisibility, or assert the appropriate quotient-and-remainder relationship with carefully stated sign behavior. Never patch correct code merely to satisfy an incorrect property.

Another tempting claim is that addition associativity holds for every checked operation sequence. Mathematically it does over unbounded integers, but intermediate overflow can make one grouping fail while another succeeds. Distinguish mathematical identities from identities of a finite checked computation. Restrict the domain or compare success/error behavior under a precisely stated condition. Property tests require more specification, not less.

Playbook: a generated case fails

Observation: a proposed division property fails for 7 and 2 even though the evaluator returns the documented quotient 3. Hypothesis A: the parser groups division incorrectly. Hypothesis B: the property assumes exact division where the language truncates. Distinguishing experiment: evaluate 7 / 2 directly and compare with ordinary i64 division, then test 8 / 2 under the property. Expected results: both evaluators return 3 for the first, while the divisible case satisfies the proposed equation. This disproves a parser explanation for that reproduction and supports a missing property precondition.

Capture the minimized counterexample, the original claim, and the revised domain. Do not delete the failing case without explanation; preserve it as evidence of the semantic distinction. Ask AI to search for a counterexample to a property before generating hundreds of tests. Then verify its counterexample manually and through execution. This uses assistance to challenge assumptions rather than rubber-stamp a test suite.

Separate an evaluation result from its presentation

The evaluator remains a pure function. The executable writes its result with fallible writeln!, flushes normal output, and reports a closed sink as an ordinary failure. Error diagnostics are best effort if stderr is unavailable. The output regression forces a broken pipe before process startup; existing corpus tests continue to establish expression semantics separately. A nonzero exit is therefore not enough to diagnose invalid syntax: read the available error category and reproduce the output conditions.

When you get stuck: independent work and tiered help

Add a table of boundary expressions: maximum plus one, minimum minus one, minimum divided by -1, negated minimum, zero divisor, and a valid near-boundary result. Specify expected error category and operator span. Next extend the finite property domain with whitespace variations that preserve evaluation. Avoid generating inputs beyond the resource limits unless the property you are testing is predictable rejection. Keep arithmetic semantics and resource semantics separate in your assertions.

Hint 1: choose the next observation

minimize a failing generated expression to the smallest numbers and operators that retain the difference.

Hint 2: narrow the experiment

compare AST grouping before comparing arithmetic values.

Worked solution

for a,b,c in a deliberately small domain, assert evaluate("(a)+(b)*(c)") equals a+b*c and evaluate("((a)+(b))*(c)") equals (a+b)*c. Parenthesize inserted negative values so your generator does not accidentally change the grammar. A review request should state the property's domain, oracle, counterexample, and remaining uncertainty.

Completed-project review and mastery

Review the five foundation projects as a progression. The calculator established explicit arithmetic contracts. The journal added valid state and persistent input. Logs added resource bounds and borrowed views. Configuration added deterministic precedence and validated types. Expressions combined recursive structure, spans, arithmetic, and layered testing. Each project moved an assumption to a visible boundary and added evidence appropriate to that boundary.

For this project's final review, run unit, integration, and documentation tests and record actual commands and outcomes. Read the resource-limit tests and identify which cases they cover; inspect the construction argument for the cases they do not enumerate. A passing finite suite is code-verified evidence for executed checks, while independent review remains pending until someone separate actually examines the work. Mastery means defending both the implementation and the limits of your claims, and proposing the next most informative experiment when uncertainty remains.

Engineering decisions and evidence

Requirements and invariants

The grammar specifies precedence, left associativity, unary minus, whole-input consumption, and UTF-8 byte spans. Arithmetic is checked. Source bytes, token count, parser nesting, and AST depth are bounded separately. Private Expr construction preserves the depth invariant used by recursive evaluation and destruction.

Chosen design and concrete habits

Lexing, parsing, and evaluation have distinct failure boundaries. The parser stores operator spans so runtime errors identify the responsible operation. Evaluation propagates typed errors with ? and uses checked operations for every arithmetic case. The lexer character expect documents a remaining nonempty valid-boundary invariant; no user syntax failure relies on panic. Doctests propagate errors rather than teaching routine unwrap.

Meaningful alternative and evolution threshold

An arena or explicit evaluation stack becomes useful for languages that must accept much deeper trees. A parser library can help when grammar recovery, many operators, or complex declarations become requirements. Direct i64 minimum literal support needs a magnitude design; it cannot be added honestly by changing one display rule. New constructors or deserializers must preserve resource invariants.

Actual checks and remaining uncertainty

Native precedence, associativity, Unicode spans, malformed input, arithmetic errors, limits, fixed corpus, documentation, and finite exhaustive small-integer properties passed in verification/native-tests.log and passed again in verification/patch001-foundations-tests.log after the patch audit. These properties use a bounded independent arithmetic oracle and are not randomized fuzzing or universal proofs. Independent review remains pending.
